activities.anchor: Mass lives in the object; weight lives in the interaction
activities.caption: file the quantities — mass or weight?
activities.name: nlMassBuckets

config.prompt: Six quantities just flew past. File each into the right bucket:

items.label: a gravitational force, pointing vertically down
the same value on the Moon as on Earth

config.why: Mass is the amount of matter — a scalar that travels with the object unchanged. Weight is a force the planet exerts on that mass, so it changes with g and is always measured in newtons.

activities.anchor: would read a sixth of its Earth value there
activities.caption: pin the Moon's pull on the gravity scale
activities.name: nlMoonPlace

config.prompt: Surface gravity is a range — Earth sits at 9.8 N/kg. Place the Moon on the scale (N/kg):
config.why: The Moon pulls with about 1.6 N/kg — roughly a sixth of Earth's 9.8 N/kg. Same astronaut, same 60 kg mass, but the weight drops from ~590 N to ~96 N.
config.context: That is why a spring scale reads a sixth of its Earth value on the Moon, while a balance reads the same in both places.

activities.anchor: are all the same law, politely anticipated
activities.caption: bet first — why do you lurch when the bus brakes?
activities.name: nlBusPredict

config.q: A bus brakes hard and you lurch forward. What is actually acting on you?
choices: Nothing — your body simply keeps its velocity while the bus slows under it
A forward-pushing force created by the brakes acting through the seat
A third-law reaction to the bus decelerating beneath you
config.why: The brakes slow the bus, not you. Until something pushes you backward, the first law says your body carries on at 90 km/h — same story as the headrest in a rear-end collision, in reverse.

activities.anchor: while you accelerate by a useful one
activities.caption: pair each force with its genuine third-law partner
activities.name: nlPartnersMatch

config.prompt: Match each force to its true third-law partner — remember: partners act on different bodies:

pairs.left: the rocket engine pushes exhaust gases backward
pairs.right: the exhaust gases push the rocket forward

pairs.left: you push the water backward while swimming
your shoe pushes the pavement backward

config.why: Every partner acts on the OTHER body — equal strength, opposite direction, different object. Equal-and-opposite forces on the SAME body are equilibrium, not a third-law pair.

activities.caption: true or false — stability, tops and bases
activities.name: nlStabilityJudge

statements.s: A tilted object topples when the vertical line from its centre of gravity falls outside its base.
statements.why: Outside the base, the object's own weight produces a moment that turns it further over — topple.

statements.s: Racing cars are built low and wide to make the centre of gravity harder to swing outside the base.
statements.why: Lower centre of gravity plus wider base: the tilt needed to leave the base is much bigger, so corners do not tip it.

statements.s: Standing on one foot doubles your base of support.
statements.why: It halves the base — which is exactly why you wobble.

statements.s: A double-decker bus fails its tilt test when the top deck is full of passengers.
statements.why: Buses pass dramatic tilt tests; a high load raises the centre of gravity, but the design keeps it inside the base even tilted.

activities.anchor: twenty times gentler on the occupants, for the same total momentum change
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the crumple-zone calculation
activities.name: nlCrumpleSpot

config.prompt: This crash-impact answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: A 1,000 kg car at 20 m/s carries momentum p = m·v = 20,000 kg·m/s.
A rigid wall stops it in 0.1 s, so F = Δp/Δt = 200,000 N.
A crumple zone stretches the stop to 2 s, so F = 20,000 / 2 = 10,000 N.
Lengthening the stop increases the force — that is why crumple zones hurt more.
Same total momentum change, one twentieth of the force: the occupants barely notice.
config.correction: Lengthening the stop DECREASES the force — F = Δp/Δt, and a bigger Δt buys a smaller F.
config.why: The momentum change is fixed; the force is its rate. Stretching 20,000 kg·m/s over 2 s instead of 0.1 s is what makes the stop twenty times gentler — the crumple zone is a time machine for the same Δp.

activities.anchor: the moment transformers appear in the magnetism chapter
activities.caption: rebuild the switch-flip sequence — field first, electrons later
activities.name: ohmFlipOrder

config.prompt: From flick to lap complete — put the story of a flipped switch in order:
items: The electric field propagates around the loop at nearly light speed
Every conduction electron in the loop starts drifting at once
One individual electron finally completes a full lap — almost an hour later
config.why: The field travels, not the electrons. Their drift speed is under a millimetre per second, so the whole loop starts moving together in milliseconds while a single electron needs the best part of an hour for one lap of a torch circuit.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — what a volt actually is
activities.name: voltCloze

config.text: A volt is a joule per %%0%%: a 12 V battery transfers %%1%% J of energy to every coulomb that passes through it, and under heavy load its terminal voltage %%2%% because of its internal resistance.
config.hint: Think energy-per-charge, the battery's rating, and what a starter motor does to terminal voltage.

activities.anchor: the quadruple-the-heat warning of the short circuit, visible on sliders
activities.caption: find the faulty line — heater resistance and power
activities.name: heatSpot

config.prompt: This heater answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: A heater draws I = 4 A on a 230 V supply, so R = V/I = 57.5 Ω.
Its power is P = V·I = 230 × 4 = 920 W.
A repair shortens the element, halving R; the current doubles to 8 A.
The power doubles too, to 1,840 W — at fixed voltage, power scales linearly with resistance.
That is exactly why a short circuit, with R collapsing toward zero, is dangerous.
config.correction: At fixed voltage the power QUADRUPLES, to 3,680 W — P = V²/R, so halving R multiplies power by four.
config.why: P = V²/R: power scales inversely with resistance at fixed voltage. Halve R → double I → the power jumps fourfold — the lesson's 12 Ω → 4 Ω example did exactly this (12 W → 36 W would be thirds; halves give fours).

activities.anchor: not a reservoir of electric fluid that drains away
activities.caption: true or false — what flows, what runs out
activities.name: flowJudge

statements.s: Current gets used up as it travels around a series circuit.
statements.why: Charge is conserved — the current is the same everywhere in the loop. What each component takes its share of is energy.

statements.s: Voltage is a property of two points, not a substance that flows.
statements.why: Current flows; voltage drives. 'Voltage flows' is the tell-tale sign of the misconception.

statements.s: A battery moves charge that is already packed into the wires; what depletes is its chemistry.
statements.why: The battery is an energy pump with a finite fuel supply — it exhausts reactions, not charge.

statements.s: A car battery holds its terminal voltage constant no matter how much current is drawn.
statements.why: Internal resistance makes terminal voltage sag under heavy load — cranking a starter can pull 12.6 V down to near 10 V.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the kettle's energy appetite
activities.name: kettleEstimate

config.prompt: A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours. Roughly how many joules of energy did it burn?
config.why: 3 hours × 2 kW = 6 kWh, and 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ, so 6 × 3.6 = 21.6 MJ.
config.context: That is why bills are written in kilowatt-hours — nobody wants to pay for 21,600,000 joules in words.

activities.anchor: a low-resistance path where the equations promised high
activities.caption: bet first — what does the bigger fuse actually protect?
activities.name: fusePredict

config.q: A 3 A appliance keeps blowing its fuse, so a friend fits a 13 A fuse 'so it stops blowing'. What did that actually change?
choices: The circuit is now protected with a safer margin
The cable can overheat and burn before the fuse ever melts
The appliance now draws less current than before
config.why: A fuse guards the cable, not your patience. Four times the design current can now cook the cable while the 13 A wire sits there unmelting — the correct move is matching the fuse to the thinnest link it guards.
